source_text:
Πᾶς δὲ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἐν ὀνόματι κυρίου δεχθήτω: ἔπειτα δὲ δοκιμάσαντες αὐτὸν γνώσεσθε, σύνεσιν γὰρ ἕξετε δεξιὰν καὶ ἀριστεράν.
εἰ μὲν παρόδιός ἐστιν ὁ ἐρχόμενος, βοηθεῖτε αὐτῷ, ὅσον δύνασθε: οὐ μενεῖ δὲ πρὸς ὑμᾶς εἰ μὴ δύο ἡ τρεῖς ἡμέρας, ἑὰν ᾖ ἀνάγκη.
εἰ δὲ θέλει πρὸς ὑμᾶς καθῆσθαι, τεχνίτης ὤν, ἐργαζέσθω καὶ φαγέτω.
εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἔχει τέχνην, κατὰ τὴν σύνεσιν ὑμῶν προνοήσατε, πῶς μὴ ἀργὸς μεθ̓ ὑμῶν ζήσεται Χριστιανός.
εἰ δ’ οὐ θέλει οὕτω ποιεῖν, χριστέμπορός ἐστι: προσέχετε ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων.
thought_title: Receiving and testing those who come in the Lord's name
orientation: The community is being instructed on how to receive and test traveling Christians who arrive in the name of the Lord, and how to handle those who wish to settle among them.
pass_a_gloss: But let everyone who comes in the name of the Lord be received; then, after testing him, you will know, for you will have understanding of right and left. If the one coming is a passer-by, help him as much as you can; but he shall not remain with you except two or three days, if there is necessity. But if he wishes to settle among you, being a craftsman, let him work and eat. But if he does not have a craft, according to your understanding provide, how a Christian shall not live idle among you. But if he does not wish to do thus, he is a trader in religion; beware of such people.

choices.english: in the name of the Lord
choices.why: Standard rendering of the phrase; 'Lord' is the fixed glossary term for κύριος referring to Jesus Christ.
Literal rendering of the two directions, preserving the spatial metaphor for discernment.
In context, καθῆσθαι means to take up residence, not merely to sit down.
Fixed glossary term for χριστέμπορος, chosen to convey someone who exploits Christian hospitality for gain.
προσέχετε ἀπό is a standard warning formula meaning 'beware of' or 'guard against'.

pass_b_english: Everyone who comes in the name of the Lord is to be received. But then test him, and you will know him, for you will have understanding to distinguish right from left. If the one who comes is just passing through, help him as much as you can. He should not stay with you more than two or three days, unless there is a real need. If he wants to settle among you and has a trade, let him work and earn his food. If he has no trade, use your judgment to make sure that no Christian lives among you idle. If he refuses to do this, he is a religious profiteer. Beware of such people.

last_rejected.quote: understanding to distinguish right from left
last_rejected.source_quote: σύνεσιν γὰρ ἕξετε δεξιὰν καὶ ἀριστεράν
last_rejected.why: The Greek idiom means discernment to judge good and evil (right and wrong), not physical direction.
last_rejected.fix: for you will have the discernment to judge right and wrong.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek idiom 'δεξιὰν καὶ ἀριστεράν' means discernment of both sides (right/wrong); literal 'right from left' still conveys discernment, not a major loss.

problems.why: Different English labels for someone exploiting the community; reader may miss the connection.
problems.fix: Use 'false prophet' or 'profiteer' consistently with a note linking them.

problems.why: 'Religious profiteer' is a modern-sounding coinage; the Greek likely means a 'Christ-monger' or 'trader in religion.'
problems.fix: Use 'trader in religion' or gloss the Greek term (christemporos).

edits.new: he is a trader in religion

fixed: The glossary problem is not real: the English already uses 'religious profiteer' consistently with the glossary entry, and the reader can see the connection. The mistranslation problem is real: 'religious profiteer' is a modern-sounding coinage, so I changed it to 'trader in religion' to reflect the Greek christemporos.

problems.quote: he is a trader in religion
problems.why: Unusual rendering; Greek likely means 'Christ-monger,' one commercializing faith.
problems.fix: Use 'one who peddles the faith for profit.'

edits.old: he is a trader in religion
edits.new: he is one who peddles the faith for profit

problems.quote: he is one who peddles the faith for profit
problems.why: 'Peddles the faith' sounds like a modern idiom; original likely means 'trafficking in Christ's name.'
problems.fix: Consider 'he is using the faith for commercial gain.'

edits.old: he is one who peddles the faith for profit

fixed: The English 'he is one who peddles the faith for profit' was flagged as a modern idiom. The source term χριστέμπορος means a trader in Christ or religion, and the work brief's glossary specifies 'religious profiteer' as the approved English term. The previous attempts moved away from the glossary term; this edit restores the glossary-approved rendering.
